articles.headline: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
keyFacts: Nvidia's board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted an affair with an executive U.S. officials suspect is a Chinese spy.
Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimated Huang has a 50-50 chance of keeping his job following the scandal.
Nvidia said Huang remains CEO during the investigation, and three House chairmen requested a briefing on November 18.
body: Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the booming AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised, and that Huang is staying on.

The question now is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the reputational damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none. Executives who survive personal scandals usually pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example example. Between 2005 and 2010, he turned HP to the top of the industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent move to make because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him from inside (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are the sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow in the coming weeks. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament especially tricky. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a spiral.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions, either by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

articles.headline: Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality
keyFacts: Heavy smog blanketed New Delhi after residents set off firecrackers during Diwali celebrations, worsening the city's seasonal air pollution.
On Monday morning, New Delhi's Air Quality Index reached severe levels above 350, posing health risks according to World Health Organization standards.
Cool weather and low wind speeds can cause the thick pollution haze to linger over the capital for days.
body: Heavy smog has blanketed New Delhi after firecrackers lit up the Indian capital during Diwali celebrations, worsening the seasonal pollution crisis.

Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, was celebrated across India on Sunday. Despite restrictions on fireworks, New Delhi residents celebrated the festival of lights with firecrackers throughout Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere.

On Monday morning, the Air Quality Index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital, categorised as “severe” and posing significant health risks, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) recommended exposure thresholds.

Last month, India’s Supreme Court put in place restrictions to limit Diwali pollution, allowing only approved “green firecrackers” under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The approved crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free.
Seasonal pollution
On Wednesday, days before Diwali, toxic air pollution in New Delhi surged to more than 30 times the WHO’s recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed.
New Delhi, home to 30 million people, persistently ranks among the world’s most polluted capital cities.
The issue is exacerbated during the winter, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing.

Vehicles account for 23 percent of New Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

articles.headline: Trump says he ‘cannot’ forgive his enemies even if it means denial at Heaven’s gates
keyFacts: President Trump stated in an interview that he cannot forgive his enemies, even if it means being denied entry to Heaven.
Journalist Ross Douthat asked if Trump could forgive figures like James Comey and Nancy Pelosi to enter paradise.
Trump stated he cannot forgive his opponents due to what they put him through, including being indicted and impeached.
body: President Trump said he “cannot” forgive his enemies and never would — even if doing so would shut him out of Heaven.
The commander-in-chief said he’d rather languish in purgatory than forgive his foes after being posed the hypothetical in a “60 Minutes” interview with correspondent Ross Douthat Sunday.
The question was raised by Douthat, who initially asked Trump if he thought he’d go to heaven when he died.
“I hope so,” a solemn Trump told Douthat. “I don’t want to go to hell.”
Douthat recalled Trump’s half-joke at the memorial, where he said “I hate my opponents and don’t want the best for them” – a sentiment at odds with widow Erika Kirk’s message of forgiveness.
The journalist then posed Trump the afterlife hypothetical.

“[A]ll you have to do to enter paradise is feel love and forgiveness for [former FBI director] James Comey, [former Speaker of the House] Nancy Pelosi, anyone who you have expressed hate for over the years. Do you think you can do it?” he asked.
The president said he finds those named to be “extremely dishonest people, very bad people, very bad for our country,” before Douthat asked him if the answer to the question is “no.”
“The answer is no,” Trump said. “I want to be honest.”
When Douthat raised the stakes, saying that in this scenario he’d be denying those who wronged him forgiveness before “the judgment throne of God,” Trump doubled down.
“Before the judgment, no. I think they were very bad people,” he said.
“I do hate some of my enemies. I think they’ve been terrible. Look what they’ve put me through, the weaponization. I got indicted. I got impeached,” Trump told Douthat.
Douthat then asked Trump how a man with “the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my lifetime” can’t bring himself to forgive his enemies.
But the president was unfazed.
“I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will,” Trump said.

articles.headline: 19 Years Later, Avatar’s Most Terrifying Episode Changed the Franchise Forever
keyFacts: Nineteen years ago, the Avatar: The Last Airbender episode "The Puppetmaster" introduced bloodbending, which allows waterbenders to manipulate the water inside living bodies.
The article stated that an imprisoned waterbender named Hama taught Katara this dark technique, leading Katara to use it out of desperation to save her friends.
The article noted that this ability later inspired terrifying villains and advanced plotlines in the sequel series The Legend of Korra.
body: For much of Avatar: The Last Airbender, waterbending seems like the most limited of the four elements for one practical reason: Its wielders need access to water. Firebenders generate their own flames. Earth is everywhere, and air is even more readily accessible. On her adventure with Aang, Katara is almost never separated from her water skin for this very reason. A waterbender in the desert is about as useful as a badgermole cub in a swimming pool.

Partway through The Last Airbender’s final season, however, that limitation becomes the basis for one of the show’s most horrifying revelations. Water is everywhere. You just have to do something terrible to access it.

Nineteen years ago today, on Nov. 9, 2007, “The Puppetmaster” introduced bloodbending, which allows a waterbender to manipulate the water inside another person’s body. Along with that extreme version of waterbending, we also learned that it’s possible to draw the water out of living things, or even the air itself.

These implications would eventually supply some of The Legend of Korra’s most frightening villains with their signature bending abilities. But its most disturbing achievement is what it does to Katara. In many ways, she’s the most virtuous of Team Avatar’s members, yet under the light of the full moon, she’s forced to learn arguably the most evil form of bending in existence.
“The Puppetmaster” turns Avatar into a horror story

“The Puppetmaster” opens with the gang telling horror stories around a campfire at night somewhere in the Fire Nation, immediately establishing a decidedly spooky vibe. An older innkeeper named Hama soon shows up and tells them that locals have been disappearing during the full moon. She offers them a safe place to stay. The story quickly evolves into something of a smalltown murder mystery where Toph is the hardnosed detective with Aang and Sokka as her hapless sidekicks.

Despite appearing a bit creepy and suspicious, Hama reveals that, just like Katara, she’s a waterbender from the Southern Water Tribe. Given the fact that the Fire Nation hunted and imprisoned most of the waterbenders from the south, leaving Katara as the only one left, Hama suddenly becomes the mentor Katara wanted for most of her life.

Hama teaches Katara that it’s possible to draw moisture from the air and extract water from plants, but doing so kills the fire lilies she demonstrates with. It’s an unsettling but practical answer to a waterbender’s most glaring struggle. Suddenly, a resourceful waterbender with no qualms about where their water comes from becomes the most potentially dangerous among the four bending styles.

By this point, Avatar had long since established that bending’s boundaries were negotiable. Lightning offered an advanced application of firebending that few could perform. Late in Book 2, Toph escaped captivity by discovering that metal wasn’t as separate from earth as everyone assumed. These breakthroughs rewarded exceptional skill and a willingness to question conventional wisdom.

Season 1 also established that certain cosmic events can influence bending. Sozin’s Comet dramatically strengthens firebending once every 100 years. Much like the tides, the waterbenders strength also stems from the moon. (It’s a little surprising that earth and air don’t get their own cosmic power boost in the same way.) That’s important because the full moon allows Hama to employ this base concept of manipulating water inside living things to its darkest potential.

On the night of the full moon, Hama reveals that she had been imprisoned by the Fire Nation for years with virtually no water. Over time, she developed bloodbending and practiced controlling the rats in her cell like puppets before applying the technique to her captors. She’s been abducting members of the Fire Nation as a form of revenge for the years of torture. The Fire Nation nearly wiped out the Water Nation's culture, so Hama sees it as their shared responsibility to return the favor. Katara refuses, which prompts an epic fight between the two where they both have to draw the water out of their surroundings to keep going.

Katara is able to resist Hama’s use of bloodbending on her, but after Aang and Sokka show up and are put in grave danger, Katara has to use it herself on Hama out of desperation. Even with the power boost from a full moon, bloodbending requires a tremendous amount of skill. A feat like this solidifies Katara’s place as one of her generation’s greatest waterbenders and is parallel to Toph discovering metalbending. The episode ends on a downer, however, with Katara bursting into tears out of regret as Hama cackles with delight that her legacy lives on.
The Legend of Korra makes bloodbending everyone’s problem

Decades later, during the era presented in The Legend of Korra, various advanced forms of bending become far more prevalent than they were previously. Republic City’s police force is composed of master metalbenders. Firebenders generate lightning to provide electricity to the city. And one particularly frightening crime family masters bloodbending in ways that are far beyond what even Hama could have dreamed.

Book 1’s primary villain is a masked revolutionary called Amon who has the power to strip a person of their bending abilities. At first it appears to be a feat similar to the energy bending technique that Aang uses on Ozai, but it’s eventually revealed that Amon is actually a Northern Water Tribe waterbender named Noatak who, like his brother, inherited the ability to use psychic bloodbending. That meant they could bend a person’s blood without the full moon and without the use of hand gestures. Noatak took it even further and developed a way to sever a person’s internal energy paths, thereby stripping them of their bending altogether.

Toward the end of the season, we learn that Noatak’s father, Yakone, was a deadly crime boss who hid his powers for years. After he was sentenced to life imprisonment, he used bloodbending to subdue Sokka, Toph, and even Aang. But in the ensuing confrontation, Aang used the Avatar state to overpower Yakone and strip him of his bending.

Yakone later had sons, Noatak and Tarrlok, and forced them to practice bloodbending on animals and eventually each other. Like Hama, he treats the younger generation’s potential as instruments of revenge. As adults, Noatak assumes the alias of Amon to lead an insurrection while Tarrlok secretly infiltrates Republic City leadership to eventually become the chairman of the United Republic Council. While they weren’t working together (Amon even went on to take Tarrlok’s bending away), they both used bloodbending to enact their father’s vengeance in very different ways.

Interestingly, after Amon succeeds in taking away Korra’s water, earth, and firebending, it’s Katara that attempts to restore them through healing. Decades after Hama forced the power of bloodbending upon her, she comes face to face with the worst damage it can cause. Of course, season 1 ends with one of the franchise’s most uplifting scenes as Korra finally connects with her past selves and Aang is able to restore her bending fully. But seeing the Avatar nearly powerless because of an obscure extension of bloodbending is one of the scariest and boldest narrative choices the series has ever made.

All of this stems from one observation a tortured old woman made: Water exists inside living things. That made the element typically associated with healing become a means of domination. Nineteen years later, Katara’s reaction still unsettles me more than the technique itself. We’re used to cheering when heroes level up and discover a new power. But when that power is as frightening as bloodbending, it’s enough to make you want to cry.

articles.headline: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
keyFacts: Linus Torvalds reported signs that the massive flood of AI-prompted software patches may have peaked.
AI bug-finding tools recently caused record patch sprees, creating more fixes than IT teams can easily process.
Torvalds stated that eBPF fixes now outpace new bug reports, hoping other Linux kernel areas reach that point soon.
body: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds.
Writing in his weekly kernel update post , the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons.
One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel.
The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.”
Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April , developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible.

Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month.
That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI .
Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us.
“This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote.
That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel.

“I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

articles.headline: Lead designer Bruce Nesmith says Skyrim was a hit because it was built on institutional knowledge from Oblivion
keyFacts: Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith said the game succeeded largely because Bethesda kept the same team that worked on Oblivion.
Nesmith stated that retaining this institutional knowledge allowed the studio to avoid past mistakes and build directly upon prior successes.
Nesmith also credited the game's success to a full, varied world offering visual storytelling, environmental diversity, and a strong sense of player freedom.
body: I don't know about you, but I'm not a huge fan of the way YouTube encourages everything becoming a video that's over an hour long and doesn't have a text version available. There's a recent video putting the original Pool of Radiance into the greater context of the history of CRPGs that's almost 10 hours long, and the odds of me watching more than 10% of it are perishingly low.

Fortunately for you, we're here to convert video to text for your edification, as with The Examined Game's comprehensive interview with Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith. Asked how a game as successful as Skyrim came to be, Nesmith emphasized the importance of keeping the team together.

If I had an actual blueprint on how to do it, I would be one rich son of a bitch. A lot of it comes down to we had the same team that had worked on Oblivion. The studio had not really changed dramatically. So we were able to deal with institutional knowledge at a high level that had been retained, which allows us to not make mistakes and build on successes. That was definitely key to it.

I think also we gave a high priority to making sure that the world was full. There was nowhere that you went where there wasn't at least something fun to see if not something fun to do. And it and it can be just little things, it can be a little vignette on the side of the road. It doesn't have to be a huge big adventure, but the visual storytelling was fantastic.

I go back to that sense of freedom once again, but we accelerated that in Skyrim compared to Oblivion. It makes the world feel rich when there's a variety of experiences. The same experience over and over and over again doesn't cut it. So you have a wealth of enemy types, you've got a lot of different treasure types and loot types, you're allowed to pick everything up in the world.

When you go see the forests, they look like forests. Then you can see the mountains, they look like mountains. And you go to ice fields and they look like ice fields, so you get a variety of environmental experiences. Each of the cities had its own characters, so they felt very different. You felt like you're experiencing something new. And the characters, the characters all felt like they had some personality to them so that you weren't just seeing cookie cutter versions of people.

I have to disagree with Nesmith on the characters, because memorable NPCs are one of Skyrim's weak spots—all those people with recycled voices and limited dialogue. But he's right that Skyrim feels full despite the absence of Ubisoft-style repeatable activities. At no point do you pick up a butterfly and get a notification that says "1/100 butterflies collected". The butterflies are just there, and you can grab them and turn them into potion ingredients if you want. Then while you're out harvesting ingredients you meet a thief or a dying orc or an NPC who points you to a sidequest, and you're off on a new journey. That's what Skyrim does well.

Nesmith goes on to say depth like that was made possible, "by having people who knew what they were doing and could hit the ground running. You didn't have to train people what it meant to make an Elder Scrolls game." Instead of laying off half the Oblivion team the moment it shipped, Bethesda kept them together. "If you look at the history of AAA studios that do sequels, you'll see that repeated," Nesmith continues. "You'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a particular percentage of the staff—was able to maintain a vision."

articles.headline: Father Arrested After Leaving Sleeping 6-Year-Old Daughter in Line for Pokémon Cards
keyFacts: John-Michael Dooley was arrested after police said he left his six-year-old daughter sleeping in a Target line for Pokémon cards overnight.
Witnesses contacted authorities after Dooley failed to return for an hour, according to the Charleston Police Department.
Dooley was charged with unlawful conduct toward a child, and police stated that the girl was unharmed and placed into protective custody.
body: A South Carolina man has been arrested and accused of leaving his 6-year-old daughter asleep outside a Target store overnight to hold his place in line for Pokémon cards, it has been reported.

According to the Washington Post , John-Michael Dooley, 35, had been waiting with his daughter outside the store this past Friday in Charleston's West Ashley district, where a throng of Pokémon fans had slowly gathered overnight in anticipation of a newly released set of the popular trading cards.

A news release from the Charleston Police Department states that officers arrived at the store around 2:30am after receiving reports of an unattended child. Witnesses at the scene told police that Dooley handed his daughter a blanket and a pillow sometime after 1am, before leaving her asleep in his spot in line. Wheen Dooley failed to return after an hour, these concerned witnesses were forced to contact the authorities.

Eventually Dooley returned to the store and was promptly arrested. In an interview with authorities, he admitted to police that he had gone home and left his young daughter unattended so that he could hold his spot in the line, according to the Charleston Police.
Dooley was then charged with unlawful conduct toward a child. Police said that the girl was unharmed and immediately placed into emergency protective custody.

This shocking act of Pokémon card-related parental neglect is in stark contrast to last week's news that the father of late Pokémon influencer Avery the Poké Kid had made a very moving plea to The Pokémon Company to create a special card in honor of his son. On his Instagram, Avery's father Christian Garcia said, "I want to make a plea to anyone, literally anyone from The Pokémon Company: If you’re watching this video, I want to figure out how to immortalize him somehow in the trading card game he loved so much." At the time of writing, there has been no official response from the Japanese company in regarding Garcia's request.

Pokémon Trading Cards, which is currently celebrating its 30th anniversary, was recently announced as one of this year's inductees into National Toy Hall of Fame , alongside Bingo, Care Bears, and the classic slide, and beating out nominees like Bop It!, mahjong, and Polly Pocket.

"Pokémon TCG’s widespread appeal and global presence are undeniable," said curator Mirek Stolee. "The Pokémon TCG successfully adapted card game formulas established by its predecessors, making it more accessible and infusing it with the lovable Pokémon creatures."

articles.headline: Trump reaffirms support for Vance’s Iran comments but says ‘a lot of people’ didn’t like them
keyFacts: President Trump backed Vice President Vance's comments attributing 2026 midterm election losses to the Iran conflict and high gas prices.
Trump said Vance's Iran comments did not affect their relationship, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Iran strike decision.
Trump will meet with Qatar's prime minister on Monday after the U.S. military announced a blockading task force against Iranian transit routes.
body: President Donald Trump backed Vice President JD Vance’s 2026 midterm elections postmortem again on Sunday evening while simultaneously saying “a lot of people didn’t like his comments.”

Vance made headlines last week after he wrote a lengthy social media post breaking down the reasons why Republicans suffered decisive losses in the midterm elections, as Democrats retook the House and Senate and picked up seats in traditionally red states such as Texas and Kansas. Public polling showed voters largely soured on the Trump administration and blamed the conflict in Iran for higher domestic prices, factors Vance cited as being primary reasons for the result.
Trump backed his vice president when he was asked about the post soon after it came out, despite Vance’s comments seemingly contradicting the president’s choice to strike Iran in February.

The president did so again on Sunday night, both when asked about the post by a reporter in person and in a separate 60 Minutes interview filmed Friday morning . In the latter, Trump told Ross Douthat, “I don’t disagree with it,” when asked about Vance’s analysis, and he also said Vance asked him about it. “You write what you want,” Trump told him.
“Has JD Vance’s comments about Iran, questioning some of those decisions, has that impacted your relationship at all?” Trump was asked Sunday night.
“No, not at all, but a lot of people didn’t like his comments, but not me,” Trump said.

He also mentioned Vance should have referenced that Trump would choose to initiate the conflict again, saying the “crazy” terrorist-sponsoring nation would “blow up the world” if it gained access to a nuclear weapon, and that “this, historically, for history, will go down as one of the best things we ever did.”
Douthat asked Trump for his personal analysis of the midterm election results, and Trump echoed much of Vance’s talking points while also saying part of the issue was his name wasn’t on the ballot.

“Well, No. 1, I was not on the ballot, but I campaigned hard for some people,” he said. “And, uh, I think if I was on the ballot, it would have been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love; there was love, we had massive rallies. You had to transfer those voters, however, to candidates that they didn’t like. But there’s something beyond that, they didn’t like the war. They didn’t like the fact that gas prices went up, because I had it down at a low. And there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”
When Douthat brought up Trump potentially endorsing a candidate in the 2028 presidential race, Trump said he “probably” would, but “not necessarily.”
“We have a tremendous bench,” he said. He mentioned Secretary of State Marco Rubio is “great” and also said “there are many others… there are some Senators that are excellent.”
“I may or may not get involved; I don’t know, maybe I’m better off not getting involved.”
“Do you think you can have MAGA without you as the leader?” Douthat then asked him.
“I think so, because MAGA is basically common sense.”
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP’S IRAN DECISION: ‘ELECTED TO DO THE HARD THINGS’
Rubio, on the other hand, said on Friday, and again on Sunday, that Trump made the right decision last February. He argued Trump was elected to “do the hard things.”

The president’s comments come one day after the United States military announced a new task force to blockade Iranian transit routes currently used for the illegal transport of goods. Trump will meet with the Qatari Prime Minister, who has been the lead mediator in negotiations between Iran and the U.S., on Monday, according to Axios .

articles.headline: Bernie Sanders warns Democrats not to spend all their time investigating Trump
keyFacts: Sen. Bernie Sanders warned Democrats against spending all their time investigating Donald Trump after taking control of Congress in January.
Sanders said Democrats must prioritize tackling affordability and supporting working-class families over focusing solely on probing Trump.
Incoming House Democrats pledged to investigate Trump, his pardons, and his allies after being sworn into Congress.
body: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Democrats should hold President Donald Trump accountable after taking control of the House and Senate in January, but warned the party not to spend too much time on probing the president and his allies.

During an appearance on NBC News' "Meet the Press," the senator said it is still important to investigate Trump administration officials for alleged corruption and illegal activity, but stressed that the priority should be tackling affordability and supporting working-class families.

Asked by host Kristen Welker if he believes that spending two years investigating Trump and his officials could jeopardize the mandate to lower prices and make life more affordable, Sanders replied, "Yes, I do."
"Do we want to hold the Trump administration accountable for their corruption, for their illegal, unconstitutional actions? Absolutely," Sanders said.
DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS
However, Sanders said that Democrats "cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump."

"At the end of the day, when you’ve got the highest rate of childhood poverty in America, of any major country, when 20% of our seniors are trying to survive on $15,000 a year, when people are scared to death that Elon Musk and the other billionaires are pushing AI down our throats with cataclysmic impacts on the economy, our privacy rights, on our health, and — and imposing an existential threat to humanity, we cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump," he said.
"We’ve got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives," Sanders continued.

Democrats campaigned on affordability ahead of the midterms, blaming the Trump administration for the soaring costs of gas, groceries, housing and healthcare. Candidates linked the rise in costs, in part, to the U.S. military's war on Iran and Trump's tariffs on countries around the world.

The Iran war, which Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other allies partially attributed to Republicans' midterm losses, led to surging fuel prices. Gas prices are nearly $1 per gallon higher than they were a year ago, according to AAA, which reported that the national average was $4.02 per gallon as of Sunday.

But after securing the majority in both chambers of Congress following last week's elections, several Democrats promised to use the power of the subpoena and investigate current and former Trump officials once they are sworn in.
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., on Sunday warned that Democrats could investigate Trump's pardons as well as allies of the president, including tech executive Elon Musk and newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
Garcia also said last week that Oversight Democrats are "ready to take on the crooks, the con men, and the Trump crime family."
"Lawyer up," he added.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to be the next House Speaker, also said last week that Democrats are "going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country."

"Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people. But House Democrats will put the American people first," he continued.
Sanders said on Sunday that the election was not just about voters wanting to stop the Trump administration’s policies.

"What I think this election was about, is the American people not only expressing disgust with Trump and his policies, but are demanding real change, no more tinkering around the edges," said Sanders. "And what the American people are saying: 'Look, we are working long hours. We’re worried about our kids. We can’t afford healthcare. We can’t afford housing. Meanwhile, the wealthiest people in America have never, ever had it so good.' And right now is the moment where the Democrats have got to stand up to big money, create an economy and a government that works for all of us," Sanders said.

The Vermont senator also accused Trump of being "mentally unbalanced" and "erratic," but acknowledged that the president is "a good politician" and "not stupid" who Democrats may be able to work with on economic and healthcare issues.

"Trump is many things. I personally believe he is mentally unbalanced, erratic, but he’s not stupid, and he is a good politician. And I think, when Trump looks out in the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage. He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does, guaranteeing healthcare to all people. Do I think we can work with Trump? Maybe. I’m, by no means, guaranteeing it. But it is certainly worth the effort," he said.

articles.headline: Trump reacts to JD Vance’s scathing midterms critique — but says he should have gone further
keyFacts: President Trump said Vice President JD Vance was right that the Iran war caused midterm losses, but added he would attack Iran again.
Vance wrote that Republicans lost control of Congress and governorships to Democrats due to voter anger over the war in Iran.
Trump claimed the war was won and predicted Iran would wither away and eventually make a deal.
body: President Trump on Sunday admitted Vice President JD Vance’s scathing midterms rant that blamed the war in Iran for Republicans’ major Election Day losses was correct, but he criticized the veep’s remarks for one specific point.
When asked if Vance’s public midterm elections post-mortem impacted Trump’s relationship with his second in command, Trump admitted that “a lot of people didn’t like his comments.”
“No, not at all, but a lot of people didn’t like his comments, but not me,” the president told reporters before boarding Air Force One in West Palm Beach, Florida.
“He was right. Other than one thing. He should have made one other statement, one which I think is very important. If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” Trump said.

“This, historically, for history will go down as one of the best things we ever did because if they [Iran] ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world. You know why? Cause they’re crazy,” he added.
Vance decried the GOP “establishment” in a 618-word post on X on Wednesday after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and a majority of state governorships.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote.
“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. I remain hopeful about our country,” Vance said.
“To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so.”
A Trump aide previously told The Post that the president was “briefed beforehand” on Vance’s statement and “did not have any issues with it.”
The White House retweeted Vance and Trump partially endorsed the appraisal, telling reporters, “I thought it was good.”
In a CBS “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, Trump appeared to sympathize with Vance’s remarks, admitting some voters “didn’t like the war.”
“They didn’t like the war. They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up, ’cause I had it down at a low,” Trump told correspondent Ross Douthat.
“And they didn’t like the war, I think mostly for that reason because I think everyone agrees that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. And they will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.

“The one thing he left out is… that I would say, and maybe he wouldn’t say it, I don’t know. I’ve never asked him really, but… if you had it to do again, would you do it? And that’s Iran. Would you go and ta… attack Iran and take away their… ’cause we won that war,” Trump doubled down while speaking about Vance’s remarks.
“That war has been won. Now they’re withering away as a country, and they’ll come, and they’ll make a deal.”

articles.headline: Has China cracked the AI data center power problem? New 800-volt DC power system is a 'world first,' offering greater efficiency and conversion than ever
keyFacts: Envision put an 800-volt direct-current power system into commercial operation at an AI facility in Inner Mongolia.
Envision claims the architecture improves electrical efficiency and reduces physical space requirements by converting grid electricity directly to direct current.
Envision expects to grow the facility to 3 gigawatts and aims for 5 gigawatts of renewable-powered computing capacity by 2030.
body: - China puts its first commercial 800V DC data center power system into operation
- Envision converts 10kV grid electricity directly into an 800V DC supply
- New power architecture combines solid-state transformers with battery storage for AI facilities
China’s Envision claims to have put an integrated 800-volt direct-current power architecture into commercial operation at an AI facility in Inner Mongolia.
The installation is located at the Galaxy AI campus in Ulanqab, where trials of its Dubhe controller and supporting energy model began in August 2026.
The company describes the deployment as the first commercial use of this configuration, although independent performance figures have not yet been disclosed publicly.
A different route from grid electricity to computing hardware
Conventional facilities generally convert incoming electricity through several stages before delivering power suitable for servers and accelerators, adding equipment and potential conversion losses.
Envision’s design instead uses a solid-state transformer to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage alternating current directly into an 800-volt direct-current distribution line.
The company says this arrangement reduces conversion steps, improves electrical efficiency and allows power equipment to occupy substantially less physical space within data centers.
A higher-voltage distribution network can also reduce the amount of copper required for cabling, potentially lowering material requirements as computing installations expand rapidly.

The architecture includes battery storage intended to respond rapidly when processor demand changes, while also supplying temporary backup during unexpected interruptions.
Envision says the storage system can provide immediate support over seconds and maintain backup capability across periods measured in several minutes.
Its controller coordinates the transformer and batteries within milliseconds, aiming to manage sudden changes in electricity consumption from GPUs.
That coordination matters because AI workloads can cause substantial swings in demand, placing additional pressure on electrical infrastructure supplying densely packed computing equipment.
The company also says its arrangement can accommodate higher-density server racks, allowing operators to install more computing capacity within a given floor area.
Ambitions extend beyond the first installation
Envision’s Galaxy facility is expected to grow to 3 gigawatts, with the company saying its eventual capacity could serve one million AI accelerators.
Envision also intends to introduce the technology through Mission Gobi, an initiative seeking 5 gigawatts of renewable-powered computing capacity by 2030.
That programme is focused on desert locations, where the company expects renewable generation and energy storage to support large computing developments.
The system has been designed to work alongside renewable electricity sources, while its batteries are intended to balance supply and changing computing requirements.
However, the company has not provided independently verified measurements quantifying efficiency improvements, installation costs or savings compared with conventional power systems.
The announcement does not also establish how the architecture performs under sustained full-load conditions or across facilities with substantially different hardware configurations.
The deployment therefore marks a commercial milestone for Envision, while the scale of its claimed operational advantages awaits detailed independent evidence.

articles.headline: How to use your laptop as a second monitor
keyFacts: Spare laptops can be converted into secondary monitors to extend or mirror displays without buying new hardware.
Built-in Wi-Fi tools like Miracast for Windows and AirPlay for Macs enable wireless display connections between compatible devices.
Deskreen software enables cross-platform connections, while HDMI video capture cards provide wired options with less lag.
body: How to use your laptop as a second monitor
Converting the device is not as easy as simply plugging in an HDMI cord, but here's what does work.

Whether you're gaming, working or simply browsing the web, adding a second monitor is one of the best ways to upgrade your workflow. Mirroring the display, which shows the same desktop on both screens, can be handy for presentations, while extending the display gives you one wider desktop. Extending the desktop into additional screen space means more visible tabs, easier multitasking and increased productivity. But making this change does not necessarily require buying a fancy setup. If you have a spare laptop lying around at home, you can make a few small tweaks to use dual monitors without going all-in on new hardware.

Converting your laptop into a second screen is fairly straightforward but not necessarily as simple as plugging in an HDMI cable. First you need to check your computer's compatibility, consider wired versus wireless options and tweak some settings on your system to smoothly extend or mirror the display. So how, exactly, do you turn your laptop into a second monitor? Here are the steps for Windows, Mac and Linux, as well as wired options via HDMI connections.
How to use a Windows laptop as a second monitor

If both your primary computer and the spare laptop you want to use as a second monitor are running Windows 10 or 11, extending or mirroring them is quite simple due to the operating systems' built-in wireless casting tools. These rely on Miracast, a functionality that enables connections between devices via Wi-Fi and requires only a quick workflow to set up.

To activate it, go to your spare laptop, open Settings, then System, then Projecting to this PC. Click Optional features, then View features, then select Wireless Display to add it. Once it installs, return to the same page and set it to Available everywhere, and open the Wireless Display app.

Now, you're ready to mirror or extend your display. On your main computer, press the Windows key + K, select the spare laptop from the list of available displays, enter the PIN and allow keyboard and mouse input. You can then choose to duplicate your screen or extend it, and you can switch anytime with Windows key + P. Keep in mind, this method of connecting your devices does require Wi-Fi on both machines, and you may experience some lag. Therefore, while it's great for presentations or organizing large numbers of tabs, it may not be the best choice for gaming.
Can I use other operating systems as a second monitor?

If both of your devices are Macs, you can use AirPlay to connect the two, but only if the MacBook is from 2018 or later. Once you've confirmed your device is compatible, go to the MacBook you want to use as the second screen, open System Settings, select General, then AirDrop & Continuity. Turn on AirPlay Receiver and then under Allow AirPlay for, select Current User. Make sure both MacBooks are signed into the same Apple ID to ensure a smooth connection. On your primary device, open System Settings, then Displays and click the plus sign from the dropdown menu to select your secondary device from the list. Decide if you want mirroring or extended display, which can be selected under settings. Like Windows' Miracast, Apple's AirPlay works over Wi-Fi and can thus have a slight delay. For a wired option with less lag, see the HDMI section below.

If connecting between two different operating systems, whether between a Windows PC and a MacBook or anything involving Linux, you will need software like Deskreen, a free, open-source tool that runs on Wi-Fi. To connect, make sure both computers are on the same Wi-Fi network, and download Deskreen on the main device. Deskreen will offer a QR code and URL. Open this on the spare laptop's browser to connect the devices. Deskreen mirrors the display by default. To extend to the spare laptop, you will need a cheap virtual display adaptor, or a "dummy plug," in your main computer's HDMI port. Like the other systems, any software that connects devices over Wi-Fi will have some lag, so consider the wired option below for gaming or other activities that rely on smoother connections.
Can I use an HDMI cable to connect my devices?

Most laptop HDMI ports are video-out only, so plugging two devices together with a cord will not directly allow you to extend or mirror displays. To work around this, get an HDMI-to-USB video capture card, which can be plugged into both laptops. Plug your main device's HDMI cable into the card, then plug the card's USB end into the spare laptop. The capture card will function as a webcam, so you can view the feed in your laptop's camera app or a free video app like OBS Studio, which runs on Windows, Mac and Linux.

If you are gaming and want to play a console without a TV, you can connect a PlayStation or a Nintendo Switch to the laptop in the same way. Again, there may be a small amount of lag but usually less than Wi-Fi-based connections, and it's unlikely to trip you up unless you are a competitive gamer. If none of these uses appeal to you, you can always use your old laptop to make a smart home hub.
