articles.headline: Return Of The Living Dead Cast Horrified By AI-Made Sequel They Were Originally Set To Star In
keyFacts: Director Richard Driscoll released an AI-generated sequel titled Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath instead of the crowdfunded film the original cast signed up to star in.
Original cast members including Beverly Randolph and Linnea Quigley expressed horror and frustration over the use of AI and their likenesses without their consent.
Cast members have encouraged financial backers to request refunds and suggested that Amazon take legal action regarding the unauthorized project.
body: Last weekend was Halloween. A night for creeps. An evening of shrieks. For some scream queen royalty, they got one of the more unpleasant kinds of frights. Richard Driscoll, who crowdfunded a sequel to the 1985 punk zombie classic Return of the Living Dead, published the new film on his website. This came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up. Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film, leaving fans and alumni more aghast at him than the flesh eating ghouls.
“This is not what we signed up for,” says Beverly Randolph on the Caffeinated Horror Dude podcast. “We got to get something out there because there’s so much hate on us right now.”

Due to some erroneous paperwork, George A. Romeroâs original Night of the Living Dead was released directly into the public domain in 1968. Because of this, it enabled any director and studio, including Romero himself, to develop âsequelsâ to the series regardless of legal claim. One of the more adored successors is Return of the Living Dead, where a gang of punk teenagers take refuge in a morgue after a melting brain eater escapes containment. It has since stood on its own as a cult classic, generating its own sequels. This includes Brian Yuznaâs grotesque Return of the Living Dead 3, which I mostly bring up because it scared the shit out of me as a kid.

In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service “DragonFLIX,” launched an Indiegogo page for “TRASH’s REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe.” Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigleyâs fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.

From what Quigley described, this movie was intended to be a blend of Sunset Boulevard and Rocky Horror. Trash, Quigleyâs character who was last seen as a nudist zombie, had become a Norma Desmond recluse, relishing in the glory days of her brain eating spree. This sounds incredible. But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be.

Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath, an almost entirely AI generated heap of rotting flesh. The results wonât surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everythingâs wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like youâre watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didnât film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout.
“It turned out to be a fiasco,” says Quigley. “I warned him, “Whatever you do, donât do any AI, because people donât like it, the fans donât like it.””

Living Dead alumni, even those who werenât attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted ‘Trashâs Revenge’ into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romeroâs original film was public domain, Return was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action.

articles.headline: Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap
keyFacts: Lando Norris won the Sao Paulo Grand Prix after capitalizing on a spin by race leader Kimi Antonelli in mixed wet and dry conditions.
Max Verstappen finished second for Red Bull despite struggling with an extreme amount of oversteer caused by a suspected car issue.
Mercedes clinched their ninth constructors' championship despite Kimi Antonelli spinning out of the lead and George Russell making a costly pit-lane error.
body: - Published
Showing off on the podium after winning the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Lando Norris made his first misstep of an afternoon that had challenged the Formula 1 drivers to their very limits.
Norris jumped off the top step, and tried to do his signature move, where he uncorks the champagne bottle by bashing it into the ground.
Except that, not for the first time, the force of his jump pushed things too far, and he smashed the bottle.
Then, holding up the shattered top to the crowd below, he stepped backwards and inadvertently put the side of his head into the sparkles blowing up from the fireworks on the front of the platform.
Red Bull drivers Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar showed no pity, and proceeded to drench him with the contents of their bottles.
In any case, Norris was fine, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella confirmed shortly afterwards, and the Briton showed no ill effects in his post-race interviews.
It was, he said, "one of the hardest races of the year in terms of focus needed every lap and therefore one of the best".
Interlagos did what it often can, and threw everything at the drivers. The race started on a wet track, which dried progressively. There was more rain at the end.

Through it all, Norris was virtually impeccable. He made new world champion Kimi Antonelli look fallible for pretty much the first time all year, and then fended off what at one point was threatening to be one of those days when Verstappen appears to have descended from the Gods.
It says a lot for Norris' performance that it overshadowed Verstappen's drive from 21st on the grid to finish second.
Actually, perhaps the race had also started with a small blemish from the man who has had to hand his title of world champion to Antonelli this year without ever really being able to defend it.
Starting from pole, Norris was relatively slow away, at least compared with the Italian, and Antonelli blasted into a lead that for a while looked as if he would not lose.
But after the Mercedes driver had built an eight-second advantage in the first 13 laps, Norris began to come back at him as the track dried.

Stopping for slick tyres a lap before Antonelli cut a seven-second deficit to nothing, and when three laps later the new champion spun at Turn One under pressure from the old, Norris was promoted into a lead that he never again looked like losing.
"A lot was thrown at everyone on a day like today, but it was probably one of our best races in terms of execution and pit stops, timing of things," Norris said.
"We boxed one lap early on to the slicks. I came out and was right behind him and forced him to push a little bit more, and obviously he went into a mistake and I could capitalise on it.
"So, in terms of always being there where we needed to be, being able to put people under pressure was a very good day for that.
"Also, from my side, just not making any mistakes, which is so easy to do on a day like today. So, great performance from the whole team. Certainly up there with one of the best I've ever had."

For both Norris and McLaren, it was a welcome return to form. They started the year slowly, having fallen behind in development on their 2026 car as they diverted resources to ensure they got their title double over the line last year.
By mid-summer, they had caught up, and Norris took two consecutive wins either side of the summer break, and was unlucky not to get another in Madrid in September.
But then other teams overtook them again and McLaren have toiled relatively in recent races, especially in qualifying.
But the combination in Sao Paulo of some new parts, the circuit characteristics suiting them, and Norris excelling in the wet in qualifying and race, put him back in the game.
In so doing, he provided a performance that served as a reminder that he has been one of the drivers of the year, even if his equipment has not always met his exalted standards.
Stella said: "When Lando operates at his best, he's definitely one of the best drivers on the grid.
"We have seen that in these conditions, like yesterday (in qualifying), it's not the first time that when you have mixed variable conditions, he kind of is one of the fastest in finding the limit.
"And you have seen this today as well, when the track was in the middle between dry and wet. It was when he was probably gaining most throughout the races on anybody else.

"He's very sensitive in understanding how much grip is available. And very, I would say, even complete as a driver, despite he's still many years ahead of him, from a technical point of view, in terms of understanding how to deploy his tools to use the grip that is available, or to adapt to the balance of the car, because you're never going to have a really perfect car.

"You're never going to have the perfect conditions. So adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you may want to possess as a driver. When there's a need to understand what's best, how to operate, he's definitely a master."
Verstappen raced with a car 'not in good shape'
For a time, it looked as if Verstappen might be in the running for a win.
A penalty for using too many engines this year left the four-time champion four places lower than the position from which he had won in similar slippery conditions at Interlagos two years ago.

So when he was up to fifth, and less than 15 seconds behind leader Antonelli, by the time the pit stops for dry tyres were looming on lap 15, with 56 still to go and more rain predicted, it looked ominous.
But once on to the slicks, Verstappen was not a threat to Norris on pace, even when heavy rain returned in the closing laps.
"That first stint went really, really well," Verstappen said. "We got very quickly back into the top 10, and the pace wasn't bad.
"But as soon as I switched to the slicks, I had an extreme amount of oversteer in the car in the high-speed corners, which made it super difficult to drive.
"So, we need to understand if something broke on the car, some kind of aero loss or whatever, because this was not normal.
"I sit here, of course, very happy with second, but at the same time, I know there was more in it if the car had been in good shape.
"Unfortunately, that was not the case. I actually did most of the race with a car that was not in good shape, and to finish second, of course, is fantastic.
"Maybe next year I'd love to start a bit further up front instead of starting from the back or the pit lane."
Mercedes back on top - but Wolff not expecting era of dominance
For a time, Antonelli looked set to celebrate clinching the title and becoming F1's youngest ever champion a week before in Mexico with a win.
But his most uncharacteristic spin ended that hope, and took him out of contention.
"Very disappointing because we were on for the win up to that point," he said.

"Also in this slicks, once I was able to get some temperature, I was getting to the rhythm, but yeah, the spin came, which still is something I need to look at because I don't know why I lost the rear so quickly as well, like no warning, nothing."
It was another bad day for team-mate George Russell, too, who had done excellent work to move up to third place right behind Norris after starting seventh.

He looked the one driver able to threaten Norris for raw pace, but his afternoon unravelled even before Antonelli's, when he spun exiting the pits and turned a 1.2-second deficit to the McLaren into 20. That was it for his hopes of a win.

Still, a fourth and a fifth place for Russell and Antonelli at the end was more than enough for Mercedes to clinch the constructors' championship. It was the team's ninth - but their first since 2021, after a difficult time through the last rule set.
Antonelli said: "I'm going to put all this aside for now because the team, you know, take the title, we take the title for the team and they all deserve it.
"I'm very proud to be part of this group and this team who has done and still does so much for me and I'm very happy for them."
Like Antonelli, team boss Toto Wolff was as focused on the lessons of the day and year as he was on the success.

He reflected on the fact that while Mercedes had dominated the first half of the season, not only have they been caught in the second, but upgrades brought to the car a few races ago did not have the expected effect.
"Look at the last few races," Wolff said. "We haven't won.

"Then today at the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away. It looked like this could be ours. But the competition has been getting tougher between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.
"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that this is going to be very difficult for us next year."
Wolff is pleased that Mercedes have found their way back to the front after struggling relatively through what was known as the ground-effect era.
But he says he does not expect this to be the start of another dominant era such as they enjoyed with Lewis Hamilton in the last decade.

"Looking back, those last four years were very difficult between getting it wrong and then kind of understanding why it was wrong and then realising, no, we didn't understand. And that was a bit back and forth," he said.
"It wasn't that bad at all when you look at the sheer numbers, but it felt not good. And the resilience of the team, the people that held together in those tough times is a factor.
"So it feels really good sealing those two titles. Not many sports teams have done that after consecutive run of championships, then a difficult spell and then coming back.

"It looks like the most maybe competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that this kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them any more, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row. And that is a completely new challenge.
"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant. And within a few races, you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road.
"It's great for the sport. I wished it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few championships. I don't think it's the reality."

articles.headline: Michael Carrick in frosty interview exchange as Manchester United boss questioned on future
keyFacts: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick rejected suggestions he might resign following a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday.
The dramatic comeback draw left United winless in their last eight league matches and dropped them into the Premier League bottom three.
United will remain in the relegation zone until they return to action against Liverpool on Sunday, November 22.
body: Michael Carrick hit back at suggestions he could resign as Manchester United boss after their draw with Aston Villa.
The Red Devils manager was involved in an awkward exchange with a reporter during a post-match interview at Old Trafford on Sunday.
Carrick was involved in a frosty exchange with a reporter on Sunday Getty
His side scored twice in stoppage time to salvage a 4-4 draw having twice trailed by two goals during the match.
However, the dramatic comeback was not enough to avoid dropping into the Premier League’s bottom three.
Meanwhile, United are now winless in their last eight league outings, claiming just one victory in the competition this term.
Their form has seen Carrick come under increasing pressure despite only signing a two-year deal as permanent boss in May.
View Tweet: https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l
Carrick clashes with reporter
Following their latest result, he spoke to Sky Sports’ Patrick Davison as part of his post-match media duties.
Their conversation soon turned frosty, though, as it focused on what could await Carrick during the international break.
The former Red Devils and England midfielder appeared to take exception to being asked about previous suggestions he could resign.
When asked if he could walk away from the role if it was best for the club, Carrick bluntly replied: “It’s not going to happen, no.”
Davison continued by asking: “What do you expect to happen? Clearly there’s going to be a conversation?”
However, Carrick continued to downplay the idea, adding: “Is there?” before the reporter probed: “You would assume so really?”
Carrick hit back at the suggestion he could resign as United boss Getty
The 45-year-old did not change his stance as the tension remained, responding: “Would you?”
Asked what he thinks, Carrick said: “You’re telling me, what do you think?”
He continued: “You know the situation, we haven’t won enough games.
“But I expect to move forward with things we’ve been working on, showing a lot of the good from today, tighten up a few mistakes and win some football matches.”
United in relegation zone
United do not return to action until Sunday, November 22 when they face Liverpool at Anfield.
As a result, they will remain inside the Premier League relegation spots for at least 15 days.
United are winless in eight Premier League matches despite their Villa comeback Getty
It marks their longest run of consecutive days inside the top-flight drop zone for 40 years.
United last spent more than two weeks in the relegation zone between September and October 1986, with their stay lasting 28 days in a row.
The Red Devils could escape the bottom three with a draw against Liverpool later this month.
Whilst they have won just one of their last ten league visits to Anfield, that victory came on their last trip in October 2025.

articles.headline: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
keyFacts: Nvidia announced an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang regarding his relationship with an AI executive and suspected Chinese agent, Alice Huang.
Jensen Huang issued a memo to employees acknowledging the affair, apologizing to his family and colleagues, and taking full responsibility.
Jensen Huang stated that he supports the independent investigation initiated by Nvidia's Board of Directors and will cooperate fully.
body: On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below.
Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA,
I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.
— Jensen

articles.headline: The world's largest telecoms firm is on trial and the outcome has global implications
keyFacts: Chinese telecommunications firm Huawei is on trial in New York over U.S. allegations of technology theft, fraud, and sanctions violations.
Huawei attributes the alleged bad behavior to isolated individuals, while U.S. prosecutors claim it was a company-wide criminal enterprise.
Huawei is now presenting its defense after the prosecution finished presenting testimony from 61 witnesses.
body: The world's largest telecoms firm is on trial and the outcome has global implications
Huawei, the world's biggest telecommunications company, is on trial in New York, accused of stealing American technology and evading US sanctions.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

In a federal courtroom in Brooklyn, the world's biggest telecommunications company is on trial. Huawei is a Chinese firm that makes smartphones, laptops, routers and all sorts of telecoms equipment that's available all over the world. The U.S. has long alleged that Huawei products pose a security risk and have banned them from being sold in the United States. And according to the U.S. government, Huawei is also a criminal enterprise. U.S. prosecutors allege that Huawei built its telecoms empire by stealing from American companies and violated U.S. sanctions by doing business in Iran and North Korea. In 2018, this all came to a head.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: Canadian authorities have arrested the chief financial officer of the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei.
SCHMITZ: In what is widely seen as an act of retaliation, China arrested two Canadians living in China, detaining them for nearly three years.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)
SCOTT SIMON, BYLINE: Late last night, China released two Canadian businessmen who had been imprisoned in China for more than a thousand days.
SCHMITZ: The U.S. agreed to a plea deal that freed Meng and released the two Canadians. One of them, Michael Kovrig, joins us now. Welcome.
MICHAEL KOVRIG: Hi, Rob. Good to be with you.

SCHMITZ: So before we begin, I think it's worth doing a thorough introduction, so our audience understands exactly who you are and why we are talking to you. In 2018, you were living in China, working as an analyst for the nonprofit International Crisis Group. Then in December of that year, Chinese police arrested you on suspicion of espionage. You were held for nearly three years. It's been around five years since you were released. Why do you think the Chinese targeted you?

KOVRIG: It's a two-part question, Rob. The first is, why did they grab Canadians, and then why did they pick me specifically? So the Chinese Communist Party directed the Beijing State Security Bureau to abduct Canadians because they wanted to blackmail the Canadian government into releasing Meng Wanzhou. It was hostage diplomacy, that simple.

As to why they picked me, I think they probably chose me because my work dealt with foreign policy and national security issues. Everything I did was transparent and open. I was well-known to the Chinese system, but it was easier for them to trump up charges than, say, if they grabbed a random shoe salesman.
SCHMITZ: So they apprehend you. They throw you in prison. Tell me about what happened to you while you were in prison in China.

KOVRIG: First of all, they arbitrarily detained me and put me in what's called residential surveillance in a designated location, which is essentially a secret detention facility, where they held me in a padded cell for about 145 days, mostly in solitary confinement, with relentless coercive interrogation in which they tried to gaslight me into confessing to crimes that I didn't commit.

And then I spent the following two years in the State Security Bureau's detention center. So during that time, I never left the cell that I was in except for consular meetings or to occasionally visit a lawyer. So for those who went through the COVID time and felt that they were a bit confined at home, I spent that entire period without being able to leave a single cell.
SCHMITZ: Wow. And now you are closely following the U.S. case against Huawei in New York. What are the details of the prosecutor's case against Huawei?

KOVRIG: So I should note - I've been following this case since before I was detained. In fact, a few days before they abducted me, I gave a television interview explaining why Meng Wanzhou had been arrested. So, for me, this is coming full circle now...
SCHMITZ: Wow.

KOVRIG: ...Right? The trial is about crimes, not about spying, right? The jury's going to determine whether Huawei broke American laws on fraud, theft and sanctions violations, and that's worth knowing for itself. The hostage-taking didn't work. Beijing held us in an effort to free Meng Wanzhou. Her signed admissions have now been read to a Brooklyn jury.

The broader implication of the trial will be whether Huawei can be trusted as a provider of critical telecom infrastructure equipment, right? For governments, whether or not to allow Huawei gear in 5G networks or to rip and replace existing equipment is a risk assessment. And the trial has bearing on whether Huawei's word can be relied on that its equipment is risky or not.

SCHMITZ: So of course, Huawei dismisses the accusations against the company, saying that prosecutors are focusing on a smattering of isolated cases of bad behavior of a few people and that this is not proof of a company-wide conspiracy to steal technology or evade sanctions. For its part, the Chinese government is calling this trial an example of U.S. economic bullying of a Chinese company. What do you say to the criticism that Huawei will not get a fair trial inside the United States, where the company's supporters say the company has been demonized and treated unfairly?

KOVRIG: This trial is being run by a judge in the Eastern District Court of New York, and it's going to be decided by a jury of 12 American citizens. That's not something that can be politicized in the same way as a decision by a government official, right? And the issue is that, you know, whether or not Huawei committed crimes - right? - lying to banks about its business in Iran, evading U.S. sanctions and stealing technology from American companies, right? Prosecutors are calling it a racketeering enterprise and trying to show that it's a 20-year pattern, not a bunch of one-off mistakes. The point we're at now, the jury's heard from 61 prosecution witnesses, and now Huawei is starting to present its defense. So we'll be getting to hear what the company has to say about that.

SCHMITZ: We're talking about the world's largest telecommunications company. You see its equipment everywhere in the developing world, whether it's routers, cellphones, you name it. What are the implications of this trial on Huawei and how it does business?

KOVRIG: One, I think, is accountability, right? Prosecutors say Huawei deceived banks in moving money through the financial system and took technology from American companies. Those are crimes with victims, whatever Huawei sells. And so a trial does something that intelligence briefings and investigative journalism can't do. It puts evidence on the public record, tested by Huawei's own lawyers, decided by a jury of citizens for every bank and government to see.

And so that ultimately has implications for every government that is deciding whether or not to use Huawei equipment, whether or not a government can take Huawei's word when Huawei says, our equipment is safe - or at least it's no riskier than any of its competitors' equipment - and that it won't allow the Chinese government to use its networks for espionage or to degrade networks or otherwise threaten critical telecommunications infrastructure. If the decision of this trial shows that you cannot take Huawei's word about that, that has implications for that risk calculation of every country that's considering whether to keep any Huawei equipment they have or get more or to rip and replace it.
SCHMITZ: That is Michael Kovrig. He's CEO of the geopolitical research firm, Kovrig Group, and is a former Canadian diplomat who served in China and the United Nations. Thank you.
KOVRIG: Thank you, Rob. It's a pleasure speaking with you.

SCHMITZ: In a previous statement, a spokesperson for the Chinese government maintained that its arrest of Michael Kovrig was in accordance with Chinese law, saying, quote, "there is no arbitrary detention at all." NPR also reached out to representatives for Huawei. They have not yet provided a response to our request for comment.

articles.headline: Nvidia Board Launches Probe After Reports CEO Was Targeted by Chinese Spy
keyFacts: Nvidia announced an investigation after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a business executive reportedly identified by US intelligence as a Chinese spy.
A committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee the probe, though Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
Jensen Huang apologized to employees in a memo, stated he will cooperate fully with the investigation, and intends to continue leading the company without interruption.
body: Nvidia on Sunday said it’s opening an investigation into whether Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive officer and founder, was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after Huang admitted having an affair with a business executive who was reportedly a Chinese spy.

The announcement of any investigation follows a series of reports that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, who is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell computing power to Chinese AI labs.

The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence agencies had Alice Huang under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law. During that surveillance, officials discovered she was also allegedly funneling information to the Chinese government in Beijing.
More from CNET

The announcement comes as Nvidia has solidified its position as a leader in the AI boom. The cutting-edge computer chips that Nvidia produces are what make AI and AI data centers possible, and that has made Nvidia one of the world’s most valuable companies by market cap.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” an Nvidia spokesperson said. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”

A committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, will oversee the investigation, the board said in a statement. The company added that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025. But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

In his own memo to Nvidia employees, Huang said he was “deeply sorry” for the affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” Huang, 63, added that he will cooperate fully with the board’s investigation.
The company had previously characterized Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
CNET’s Katelyn Chedraoui contributed to this report.

articles.headline: Iran downplays new U.S. task force aimed at disrupting land routes
keyFacts: Iran's military dismissed U.S. Central Command's new Task Force Iron Gate, aimed at disrupting Iranian trade routes, as wordplay.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said indirect negotiations with the U.S. halted due to shock from U.S. midterm election results.
President Trump said resuming U.S. attacks on Iran is highly unlikely if negotiations with Tehran make progress.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Central Command also announced the creation of Task Force Iron Gate, which is supposed to extend the success of the naval blockade to overland routes of trade. The group will be tasked with preventing military technology and illegal revenue streams from entering or exiting Iranian borders, including via the Caspian Sea, but it was unclear if any military force would be brought to bear. Iran's military on Sunday dismissed the new task force as "word play."

- The U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday it is offering up to $20 million and possible relocation in exchange for information about Iran's nuclear program, its facilities, equipment or personnel.
- President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz
Iranian foreign minister says negotiations halted after U.S. midterm elections
Iran's top diplomat said mediators working to broker a deal between the U.S. and Iran haven't traveled since America's midterm elections last week, citing "the shock" of the election results.

"For the past few days, there has been no more travel [by mediators], and the reason for this is the shock that the election results in the United States have caused to everyone," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday on Iranian state television.

"We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward," Araghchi added, in reference to the Republican Party's heavy losses.
Calling for patience, he said it would "take some time before the atmosphere is favorable for the resumption of mediator travel."

Various regional powers, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been trying for months without success to bring a definitive halt to the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran in late February. Although outright fighting has largely subsided, Iran has continued its efforts to blockade the vital Strait of Hormuz, while the U.S. has maintained a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
CBS/AFP
Trump says U.S. resuming attacks against Iran is "highly unlikely" if talks progress

President Trump said Sunday that resuming attacks on Iran was "highly unlikely," telling CNN in an interview that he believed it wouldn't be necessary to order the U.S. to return to fighting if negotiations with Tehran progress.

Washington and Tehran for weeks have been engaged in indirect, mediated negotiations to end the conflict that has drawn on since February. But talks have stalled as the two sides failed to reach agreements on key issues, like reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear capabilities. Both have put forward proposals with different sets of conditions in attempts to strike a deal.
Mr. Trump told CNN's Jim Sciutto that resuming an all-out war against Iran "depends on whether or not [Iranian leaders] sign a very strong agreement.

"The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary," the president said. "They're a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don't know how hard I hit them."
Mr. Trump will speak with 60 Minutes in his first sit-down interview since last week's midterm elections Sunday night at 7 p.m. ET/PT on CBS.
UAE says it rescued 22 crew members from cargo ship fire in Sea of Oman

The United Arab Emirates National Guard said it rescued 22 crew members from a cargo ship that caught fire in the Sea of Oman, without specifying what caused the fire or identifying the vessel. The crew members were all of Arab nationalities, the National Guard said.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, a British military organization that monitors maritime security incidents, said Sunday that a tanker caught fire on Saturday about 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, prompting the evacuation of its crew. It was unclear whether it was the same ship whose crew the UAE had helped evacuate.

On Saturday, U.S. forces disabled a St. Kitts-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, saying it had attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iran. Separately, the Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had struck mines in the area of the Strait of Hormuz. It did not identify the vessels' flags or destinations.
CBS/AP
Iranian foreign minister says it's "time for the White House" to make a choice in negotiations
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that it's "time for the White House to make its own [choice]" about how to proceed as negotiations to end the war stretch on into a fifth week.
"American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own," Araghchi said in a social media post.

"Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results," the post continued. "Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell."

Araghchi previously said that, during mediated, indirect talks with the U.S., Iran had presented a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. agreed to certain conditions.
Houthis claim attack on Riyadh financial district damaged Aramco skyscraper

Yemen's Houthis on Sunday claimed responsibility for an attack on the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, which witnesses said caused damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier Sunday that its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions.

In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group carried out four military operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Saree said the Riyadh airport was targeted in addition to the financial center, Aramco oil storage tanks, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.

He said the Houthis were responding to attacks in recent days on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and at a market in southwestern Yemen, which he said left dozens dead or wounded and blamed on Saudi Arabia.
Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.
"Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," one witness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.
One witness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said there were no casualties at the Aramco facility.
AP/AFP
Israel's defense minister says Iran mission "not complete"
Israel's defense minister hinted at a resuming attacks on Iran on Sunday, saying the "mission is not complete."

"With regard to Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons -- alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Israel Katz said.
He also warned the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon to not join Tehran in retaliating against Israel.

"We will not withdraw from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and if the terrorist organisation Hezbollah chooses to join Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer extremely severe blows," Katz said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose political bloc failed to reach a majority in the country's elections, has previously suggested he wants to resume attacks on Iran.
However, on the eve of the midterm elections President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper he had no plans to strike Iran.
CBS/AFP
Saudi oil giant's building damaged by intercepted rocket, authorities say

Witnesses in the Saudi capital of Riyadh said they heard a loud explosion Sunday morning and described damage across multiple floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District Some floors appeared to be heavily damaged.
The witnesses spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions early Sunday, accusing the Houthis of launching the weapons.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attempted attack resulted in "falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building." It added that there were no casualties.
CBS/AP
Iran's military dismisses new U.S. plan aimed at curbing ground shipping
Iran's military has dismissed the U.S.'s new task force which aims to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes as "wordplay."
In a statement to Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, a Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman said Tehran had made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours.

"The Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, the Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach," Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency.
CBS/AFP
Dozens killed in Saudi strikes in Houthi-held region in Yemen, Houthis say
Houthi authorities said Sunday that Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's revived civil war.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

The death toll from the Saudi-led coalition's strikes on Al-Shariya village located east of Yemen's capital Sanaa has risen to 33, with 39 people wounded, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said on Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."
"According to the near-final figures, the dead include 12 men, 8 women and 13 children, while the injured include 16 men, 10 women and 13 children," Alasbahi said.

Saudi Arabia, fighting in Yemen in support of the internationally-recognized government, has not commented on the report. The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh province.
The Iran-backed Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched multiple missile and drone attacks against Saudi troops and infrastructure both in the Gulf kingdom and Yemen.
Yemen slipped back into war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the conflict in the Middle East.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has expanded its attacks against the oil-rich kingdom.
U.S. forces disabled commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman, CENTCOM says

U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, U.S. Central Command said.

A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St.Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, which disabled the ship after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, CENTCOM said.
"All mariners transiting near Iranian coastal areas or surrounding waters are advised to heed blockade warnings from U.S. forces," CENTCOM said.
Earlier Saturday, CENTCOM said "strict enforcement" of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz continues.

Iran established a chokehold on the strait, a vital strategic waterway in global trade, at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October.
-CBS/AP
U.S. launches new task force to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes

In what the U.S. military is calling an expansion of the naval blockade, U.S. Central Command announced a new task force Saturday aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items like military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

The U.S. said the task force will be made up of about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, and will be tasked with the goal of "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."
The announcement made no mention of how the task force would be carrying out its goal, including whether any military operations will be involved.

China, Iran's largest trade partner, has taken to conducting commerce over land, especially by train across central Asia due to the blockade on Iranian ports. The U.S. said the blockade has prevented some $25 billion in Iranian crude oil from being sold, much of it in Asia.

In addition to China, Iran has conducted large amounts of trade over land and via the Caspian Sea with Russia. The landlocked Caspian Sea has proven especially advantageous with a direct route between southwest Russia and northern Iran. Tehran is located just 80 miles south of the Caspian Sea.
Whether any U.S. ships could take to the Caspian Sea was again unclear. CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard lifts self-imposed missile-range limit

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-proclaimed limit of 1,200 miles on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets amid fears of renewed all-out war.

The comments by the spokesman of Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country's supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini, warned "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.
Asked at a Tehran press conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, "That restriction has been lifted for us."
He did not say whether Iran had missiles capable of exceeding the limit, saying only Iran would "demonstrate these capabilities in practice" rather than make statements.

Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 1,200-mile limit — a range that puts parts of Greece and the Balkans, the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt within reach. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran's space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.

The Iranian military, meanwhile, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had hit a naval mine and caught fire. It did not identify the nationality or destination of the tanker, which it said had turned off its navigational beacon and was sailing in a "prohibited area."
22 killed in Saudi strikes on Yemen's Sanaa province, Houthis say
Saudi strikes killed 22 people, most of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's civil war, Houthi media said on Saturday.
More than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country, according to the U.N.

"The number of victims of the Saudi enemy warplane massacre in the Al-Shariyah area ... has risen to 22 citizens, most of them children and women, while the number of wounded has risen to 30," the Houthis' Saba news agency said.
The Iran-backed group's Al-Masirah TV provided the same toll.
Saba said earlier Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."
The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched toward Riyadh province.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis said Saudi airstrikes were to blame, while Yemen's government forces accused the Iran-backed group of having fired a ballistic missile at the site.
AFP/CBS
Iranian army says forces learned from war with the U.S.
Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February, Iranian state media reported on Saturday, citing an army spokesman.

"Today, the Islamic Republic's armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war," spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the state news agency IRNA.
"They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence."
CBS/AFP
Trump confirms U.S. carried out more "minor strikes" on Iran
President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" in Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm Island on the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mr. Trump was asked whether the U.S. carried out more strikes on the island.
"I don't want to talk about it," the president said. "We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe 5."

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm island, added that there was no official information on the damage. Iranian state television also reported two explosions on the island.
White House offers up to $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program
The Trump administration is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program, the U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday.
The reward, which is being administered through the State Department's Rewards for Justice national security program, also comes with "possible relocation" for the tipster.

The State Department said it is calling for "information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above."
Since the U.S. launched its war with Iran in February, President Trump has repeatedly reiterated that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

In its reward form, the State Department noted that according to the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran's uranium stockpile is believed to include uranium that has been enriched to 60% purity – "a level that is a short technical step from" the 90% level required to produce nuclear weapons.

"Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level," the State Department said in its Rewards for Justice post. "Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons."
Iran suspended IAEA inspections following on Iranian nuclear facilities by the U.S. and Israel.

"The regime's lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges," the State Department said Friday.
U.S. coordinates with Canada to target Iranian digital asset providers
The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.
Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.
The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.
"Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.
Rubio to likely face questions about Iran at G7 foreign ministers meeting
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to embark on his first post-midterm foreign trip to attend a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in France next week.
He'll likely face questions about the Trump administration's policies, namely in Iran, after in elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.
The State Department said Friday that Rubio would travel to Paris to meet his counterparts from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.
Houthis say 30 people killed or wounded in Saudi strike on market
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that a Saudi strike on a market in southwestern Yemen had killed or wounded 30 people.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said the "horrific massacre" had "resulted in the martyrdom and injury of more than 30 citizens."

The Houthis' political bureau said in a statement carried by Saba: "It is regrettable that these documented Saudi crimes have become like a forgotten file in the drawers of the United Nations and the so-called international community."
Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing and wounding "dozens of civilians" in attack on market

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Friday that the Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognized government had targeted a market in the southwest of the country, killing and wounding "dozens of civilians."

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that Saudi aircraft struck the Al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate on Friday "with three airstrikes, leaving dozens of civilians dead and wounded."
"These brutal crimes will not go unanswered and unpunished," he added.
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday, meanwhile, that air defense systems had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard say they have intercepted a U.S. drone in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday to have destroyed another U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement carried by the state TV network IRIB, the IRGC said a U.S. MQ-1 drone was "intercepted and destroyed over Qeshm Island by the IRGC's new advanced air defense system."

The IRGC claimed this was the 16th American MQ-1 drone it had intercepted during the war, and the second in two days. Iranian forces have also claimed to have shot down other U.S. drones, including more than two dozen of the more advanced, and more expensive MQ-9 Reapers.
Greek shipping firm says crew member killed in suspected missile strike on oil tanker
A seafarer was killed in an explosion caused by a suspected missile attack on an oil tanker Thursday in the Persian Gulf, a Greek company that manages the vessel said Friday.

The MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, which was not carrying cargo, was hit Thursday as it sailed toward Bahrain, management firm Velos Tankers said in a statement, according to Reuters.

"The company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the statement said.
Velos said, according to Reuters, that no crew members were injured and they managed to extinguish a fire on the ship caused by the blast.
The vessel was brought to Khalifa Bin Salman Port in Bahrain, and the damage to its hull was still being assessed, Reuters said.
Saudi-led coalition fighting Houthis in Yemen says drone intercepted in Mecca region

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that it had intercepted a drone in the region of Mecca, Islam's holiest city, following repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Yemeni rebels.
"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesman, wrote on X, without elaborating.

Since the breakdown of a truce in July, Saudi Arabia has traded blows with the Houthis, who have retaliated with strikes on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites that killed at least 20 people in October.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting the holy cities of Mecca or Medina in Saudi Arabia and said they would not do so.
On Thursday, the Saudi coalition said it intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis at the Medina region, a claim rejected by the Iranian proxy group as a "blatant and grave falsehood."
CBS/AFP
Adviser to Iran's supreme leader says Tehran now "one of the main architects" of Mideast security
The Iranian supreme leader's adviser on international affairs, Aliakbar Velayati, said Friday that Iran was now "one of the main architects" of security in the Middle East.

Referring to how the U.S.-Iran war has changed the region in a series of posts on X, Velayati said that a "tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia swept up the Israeli and U.S. elections," and that "Iran is now one of the main architects of the regional order, a reality that cannot be erased or replaced."

Iran is a "bridge between the Persian Gulf, Central Asia, the Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added, saying that "any energy or transit corridor seeking to bypass us will either be costly or unstable."

"The domino effect of crises, from Gaza to the Red Sea and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone will experience collective insecurity."
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since on Feb. 28.
Tanker hit by explosion in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. naval agency says
A tanker was hit by an explosion Thursday in the Strait of Hormuz, a British navy agency said Friday.

The master of a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz near Oman's coast reported "an explosion at the waterline" of the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said, adding that the crew were all safe and the ship was "still under its own power and is continuing on its voyage."

Iran's state media reported Thursday that five oil tankers and a tugboat had caught on fire in or near the strait after hitting sea mines. It was unclear if the UKMTO report was in relation to one of those incidents claimed by Iran.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Friday, in a statement carried by state media, that two more oil tankers had hit mines and caught on fire in or near the strait.
President Trump has accused Iran of lying about such incidents in an effort to drive up energy prices.
Trump holds a phone call with Qatar's emir, a key mediator in negotiations with Iran

President Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, a U.S. official confirmed to CBS News Friday, amid a diplomatic push to avoid a new round of major hostilities.

Their discussion, which the White House had not provided any information about by Friday morning, came as Iran's top diplomat made his own calls Thursday to counterparts across the Persian Gulf aimed at maintaining "stability in the region" amid concerns in many Gulf capitals that Mr. Trump will order major new U.S. strikes.

Al Thani received a call from Mr. Trump, according to a statement from the emir's office, during which the pair discussed "the latest regional developments, particularly diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."
The emir "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and relying on diplomatic means to settle disputes and prevent further escalation," the statement said.
U.S. gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. Why are fuel costs falling?
Motorists could soon see U.S. gas prices drop below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News he expected the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday and early Friday morning, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped over the last week, thanks largely to market expectations that the U.S. would underscore public dissatisfaction with the Iran war and pile pressure on the Trump administration to make a deal to end the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Saudi-led coalition intercepts 2 missiles launched by Houthis

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Friday that air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.
"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the statement said.
Iran says 2 tankers hit mines, caught fire in and near Strait of Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement carried by state media Friday that two oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz, a day after Tehran claimed five other tankers had met similar fates.

"Two violating oil tankers — one east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within the Strait itself — that attempted to transit via an unauthorized route struck mines," the IRGC said in a statement, according to state news outlets.

"These two tankers had deactivated all their navigation and identification systems. Supported by the aggressive and terrorist U.S. military, they attempted to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorized path; however, upon striking mines, they caught fire and were immobilized," the statement said.
On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz in similar incidents.
There has been no confirmation of any of the incidents from maritime officials, and President Trump has accused Iran of making up such attacks to drive up global energy prices.

A U.K. naval agency said earlier this week, however, that despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe, there were at least 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region during October alone, a record high.

Since the war began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran has sought to control traffic through the strait, a key passage through which, before the war, about a fifth of global crude oil supplies would typically pass. In response, the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers through the strait, which, along with other routes has helped bring shipments from the Gulf back up to or at least near to pre-war levels, but ships continue coming under attack.
CBS/AFP
Putin and Iran's security chief discuss building an oil pipeline from Russia to Iran

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between the two countries, including with the potential construction of a pipeline for Iran to import Russian gas.
Speaking with journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to the Iranian embassy in Moscow.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iranian state TV.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighboring countries."
Despite being a major producer, Iran has long suffered natural gas shortages, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
CBS/AFP
Trump touts imminent decision on whether he'll order new strikes on Iran
President Trump said Thursday that people will soon know his decision on whether to order a new round of U.S. strikes on Iran.
Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed it would take Iran 25 years to rebuild the country from the damage already inflicted during the war.
The president said he didn't want to bring further destruction to the country, but he may not have a choice.

Mr. Trump kept the possibility of a major new U.S. assault on Iran on the table in the run-up to the midterm elections this week, but hadn't renewed the threat since his Republican Party's dismal performance in the vote, which he acknowledged was, at least in part, a repudiation of the war.
Mr. Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening, as U.S. ballots were counted, that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran.

articles.headline: Ocarina of Time remake datamine suggests Master Quest is on the way
keyFacts: Dataminers found references to the Master Quest mode in the files for the new Ocarina of Time remake.
Dataminer OatmealDome stated that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC and features a mirrored world and modified dungeons.
Nintendo has not officially announced DLC or the release of Master Quest for the remake.
body: Ocarina of Time's notoriously tricky Master Quest mode could be making a comeback in the new remake.
Dataminer MrCheeze shared a list of strings from the remake's files on Bluesky, several of which tie the tag "MQ" to dungeons like Dodongo's Cavern.
In a follow-up, as spotted by TheGamer, they pointed to further entries, including "HasMQ", "IsMQModeExist", "NewGameMQ", and "ReleaseMQ".

Fellow dataminer OatmealDome added on Twitter/X that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC, rather than arriving in an update, though "the data is incomplete". "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.
— MrCheeze (@mrcheeze.github.io) November 6, 2026 at 2:23 PM

If you've not played it, Master Quest is a remixed version of Ocarina of Time with rearranged dungeons and tougher puzzles. It first appeared as a bonus disc on GameCube, then came back in 2011's Ocarina of Time 3D, which unlocked it after you finished the main game. That version also mirrored the whole world, which matches what OatmealDome has found, and had enemies deal double damage.
[Ocarina of Time] #ootspoilers
There is data in the game files for Master Quest. It will be unlocked by *owning DLC* - it is not just an update.
The data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly).
— OatmealDome (@OatmealDome) November 7, 2026

As with any datamine, there's no guarantee it'll ever see the light of day. Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for the remake, and it's not clear whether Master Quest would be free, like it was on 3DS, or paid.
The Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on 5th November. Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

articles.headline: Trump Floats Using UFC Henchmen To Beat Up Journalists In Wild Repost
keyFacts: Donald Trump reposted an AI-generated video depicting UFC fighters physically assaulting journalists inside the White House press briefing room.
Trump had previously announced offering UFC boss Dana White the role of White House press secretary.
Dana White reportedly declined the job offer, but he said he is meeting with Trump on Monday.
body: President Donald Trump promoted a video showing mixed martial arts artists attacking journalists on Sunday less than 24 hours after pitching his pal and UFC boss Dana White to serve as the next White House press secretary.

Trump, in a wild Truth Social repost, shared an AI-generated animated clip from X that depicts White slamming his hands on the podium inside the White House press briefing room and declaring that he “bought help” in the form of several UFC brawlers before they assault journos for simply asking him questions.
“Is Trump a threat to democracy?” asks one journalist in the clip, which appears to have been made in the style of “Family Guy.”
“Khabib,” replied White, essentially summoning Russia’s Khabib Nurmagomedov, who grabs the journalist by his shoulders and takes him down to the ground.

“Let’s talk now,” Nurmagomedov tells the reporter while pinning him down on the floor. (It’s worth noting that the fighter once had a cozy relationship with Vladimir Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, the leader of Chechnya whose government has long been accused of human rights violations against journalists.)

Elsewhere in the clip, another Russian fighter, Islam Makhachev, is seen grabbing and carrying out a crying reporter who says he doesn’t “feel safe” before suggesting he’ll be sent to Dagestan for up to three years.
White also summons Brazilian-American fighter Amanda Nunes and America’s Kayla Harris who begin to pull at the arms of a blue-haired reporter with a septum ring who asks about Trump’s pronouns.
“This is fascism!” the reporter shouts while running out of the room while another fighter kicks someone square in the face.

Fighter Josh Hokit later grabs the mic from White when a reporter asks him about a possible Michelle Obama presidential bid and — much like he did on the South Lawn during the UFC’s Freedom 250 event in June — declared that the former first lady was “a man,” leading to a face palm from the UFC boss.
The clip concludes with Trump asking White how the briefing went after looking out at the room full of seemingly unconscious reporters, broken chairs and destruction.
“Fiery, but mostly peaceful,” White said.
“Beautiful,” Trump replied.

The assault-laden clip arrived on the president’s timeline after he used his social media platform Saturday to announce that he offered White, whom he described as a “violent fighter and warrior,” to be the next press secretary after Katie Zacharia’s trainwreck five days on the job.
He noted he requested White bring “assistants” with him “even though some are not from our country” before naming Nurmagomedov, Makhachev, Nunes, Harris and others who made careers out of the UFC.

White — who helped bring the UFC’s controversial Freedom 250 event to the White House’s South Lawn in June — has reportedly declined the job offer, although he later told reporters at a news conference he was meeting with Trump on Monday at the White House.

articles.headline: 2026’s Games You Should Play Before The Game Awards, Described In One Sentence
keyFacts: GameSpot staff published a list of video game recommendations to help players choose favorites before The Game Awards.
The article highlights various titles across multiple platforms, including major releases and smaller indie games.
The recommendations feature one-sentence descriptions from staff members explaining why each game is worth playing.
body: As is always the case, there is no shortage of great games to play. That can make picking your favorites--or voting for categories in something like The Game Awards--a challenge. With this year's awards just about a month away, we're reflecting on what games we've loved this year to offer up some quick suggestions on what you should consider playing before casting your votes.

Below, we've rounded up one-sentence recommendations from our staff. Our goal here was twofold: recognize the games we're individually considering for Game of the Year, whether or not they're well-known, and also spotlight some of the smaller games we loved that you might have missed or never even heard of.
Mark Delaney
Retro Rewind: Video Store Simulator
Retro Rewind
Platforms: PC
My favorite of all job sims is this one about running a video rental store in the '90s, and it just got a huge update that adds video games to your inventory.
See at Steam
Big Walk
Platforms: PC, PS5, Switch 2
Bring 1-11 buddies on a hefty hike across a puzzle-filled island primed to make lasting memories.
See at Steam
Control Resonant
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5
What if Remedy took the reins from Sucker Punch and made a new Infamous, complete with the Finnish studio's unique brand of weird?
See at Steam
Far Far West (early access)
Platforms: PC
Take the exciting core of Helldivers 2, but put it in a Western with all the cartoonish whimsy you'd expect from the team behind Pumpkin Jack.
See at Fanatical
Marathon
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5
Bungie's suspenseful extraction shooter feels so damn good--this is Bungie , after all--but its art direction and worldbuilding ensure it looks even better.
See at Steam
Jessica Cogswell
Fields of Mistria
Fields of Mistria
Platforms: PC

I've argued--repeatedly--that Fields of Mistria is the greatest farming life-sim of all-time, surpassing even Stardew Valley, thanks to its '80s to '90s shōjo anime-inspired art direction, blush-inducing romances, and overall gameplay loop.
See at Steam
The Blood of Dawnwalker
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5
Okay so imagine The Witcher but with good combat, a fantastic time management system that prevents the game from feeling overwhelming, way more heart, and vampires.
See at Fanatical
Paralives
Platforms: PC

This life-sim is in early access and still has a ways to go, but it's the closest thing we've gotten to a true competitor for the Sims and I'm already so impressed by its gameplay and style, as well as the development team's commitment to its strange worldbuilding.
See at Steam
Meccha Chameleon
Platforms: PC, Switch 2

I'm not usually the type to play the "latest viral trend" when it comes to games, but I'm so glad I picked up Meccha Chameleon and got to experience how joyful and creatively rewarding this silly little "friendslop" title is.
See at Steam
007: First Light
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5

Even if you don't care about James Bond or have little knowledge of his robust history, I highly recommend 007: First Light if you want a perfectly paced, sleuthy action game that makes you feel like a total badass.
See at Fanatical
Darryn Bonthuys
Denshattack
Denshattack
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5, Switch 2
Kickflip a train, take down an evil corporation, and lock in for a cel-shaded blast of high-energy fun in this colorful and funky on-rails adventure.
See at Fanatical
Onimusha: Way of the Sword
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5, Switch 2

Onimusha: Way of the Sword shines in combat, and if you want a game where you can creatively flex your combat chops against bosses that'll test your parrying skills, this samurai showdown is an easy recommendation.
See at Fanatical
Vampire Crawlers
Platforms: PC, Xbox Series X|S, PS5, Switch 2, Switch, Mobile

Proving that it's not a one-hit wonder, Poncle has delivered a follow-up to Vampire Survivors that's deliciously entertaining and easy-to-learn--this captivating combo-powered dungeon crawler will hoover up all your free time.
See at Steam
Chris Pereira
Forbidden Solitaire
Forbidden Solitaire
Platforms: PC
What if solitaire, but it's presented with a very authentic-looking '90s-video-game-style presentation of a creepy game with demonic undertones?
See at Steam
Esoteric Ebb
Platforms: PC

A genuinely hilarious Disco Elysium-style text-based RPG adventure through a remarkably well-realized fantasy world full of "I can't believe they thought to account for that decision I might make" moments.
See at Fanatical
Over the Hill
Platforms: PC
A deeply chill exploration game that manages to strike just the right balance of engaging driving mechanics and relaxing vibes.
